title: Sacred theology is a practical habit that teaches how to worship God and reach eternal life
english: Book I. On the nature and constitution of sacred theology. Chapter 1. On the definition of theology.

Theology is a practical habit of the intellect, fully sealed by the mystical Holy Spirit from the divine disclosure in the Holy Scriptures, teaching a person on the Spirit's way — according to age, calling, and the measure of his own faith — the manner of worshipping God and of obtaining eternal life, unto the glory of God.

Scholion. First it is asked what the word theology properly signifies: whether in Holy Scripture one reads a God-speech or God-discourse — that is, the reason or speech of God by which we are instructed by God — or the reason, speech, or mental conception about God and divine things formed from the Scriptures by the power of the Holy Spirit. It is taken here in both senses.

For most weightily blessed Irenaeus says that no one can truly know God unless God himself teaches; from ([[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]): It is written in the Prophets, And they shall all be taught by God. Whoever therefore has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me. For it is not left, says Hilary in book 7 On the Trinity, to human eloquence to speak of the things of God by other words than the speech of God. All other things are narrow, shut in, hindered, and obscure. If anyone wants to demonstrate this by other words than those by which it was spoken by God, either he himself does not understand, or he leaves it not to be understood by his readers. From book 1 On the Trinity: When the discourse is about the things of God, let us grant the knowledge of himself to God; let us serve his speech with pious reverence. For he is a fit witness for himself who is not known as to himself. Let the mystery of heaven, says Ambrose in book 5, letter 31, be taught me by God himself who made it, not by man who has not known himself. To whom should I rather trust concerning God than to God?

Yet lest some fanatic abuse Christ's saying in ([[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]), here is worth considering the exposition which Urbanus Regius, a serious theologian of the past age, has in the body of doctrine to Julius on formulas for speaking carefully, under the ninth title. We, he says, do not rashly produce this place. For by the unskilled it is tossed about as an encomium of ignorance. And here they think they have a word of God by which all the liberal arts and even the studies of theology themselves may be exploded. Christ sufficiently explains this place in John 6: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. And it is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught by God. Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me. Here Christ speaks of that common doctrine necessary for all who are to be saved, by which we acknowledge Christ to be the Son of God made man for our salvation, and believe in him as our only Savior. By this doctrine certainly all the elect are illuminated; and those who lack it will be condemned. But there is also in the church another learning, which is called the gift of prophecy, with which gift not all Christians are endowed, but those who are set over churches for teaching, that they may expound the Holy Scriptures unto edification, exhortation, and consolation, of which mention is made in ([[1 Corinthians 14:1-5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:1-5]]). This gift is not common to all believers — to tailors and cobblers and apostles alike. Those who lack it ought not to teach in the church, but reverently to hear those who teach, as the Apostle says: If there is no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church, and let him speak to himself and to God.

Indeed the word theology is not read expressly in the Scriptures except for its cognate in the title of the Apocalypse, where John the Evangelist is called Theologian in the strictest sense, as one who asserted the divinity of the Word both by the Gospel history and by his Apocalypse. Yet the term is frequented by the ancient fathers, by profane writers, by the schoolmen, and finally by more recent theologians. Nor is it necessary that a technical vocabulary exist in the Scriptures, because they do not propose the formulas of arts and disciplines, but the things to be believed unto salvation.

title: Theology is called sacred over against profane science, and is a practical habit aiming at faith and eternal life
english: Why is it called sacred? Because as something set apart it is distinguished from the profane — whether from natural theology, which is known under the light of right reason and is a part of true philosophy, or from the superstitious, which is born from the blindness and hallucination of human reason and is a part of falsely so-called knowledge and empty deceit ([[1 Timothy 6:20 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:20]]; [[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]).

Is it a practical habit of the intellect? That it is a habit of the intellect no one will easily deny who at least acknowledges it as a doctrine or discipline. But whether it is a practical habit, the opinions of theologians differ, both of the older and of the more recent. And it is worst of all that the papal schools dispute this ineptly and less theologically — though not without sharpness and subtleties — presupposing philosophical disputations and afterward laboring over the accommodation of theology, while they do not have Scripture as companion.

Among the more recent, most follow a middle opinion, some the first, but the chief and leading men seem to embrace the last, by the argument of the analytic order in which they treat theology — as Melanchthon, Luther, Calvin, Bullinger, Ursinus, Keckermann, and lately William Ames the Englishman, professor at Franeker, Dr. Constantijn L'Empereur, professor at Leiden, and others. To this last opinion we cast our vote in this way: first we explain the terms, then we confirm it by reasons. The terms are (1) theology, (2) practical habit, (3) practice. By theology here we do not understand that which is God's own, as is plain from question 1, but that which is prescribed to us concerning the kingdom of God. And a practical habit is so called denominatively, as the intellect itself is, because of its extension to practice.

So we prove it. First, by clear testimonies of Scripture that express the final end both of the Gospel (concerning the doctrine of the law there is no doubt that it is practical) and of the system in which the doctrine of the Gospel is handed down summarily and methodically arranged: ([[John 20:31 >> Bible:John 20:31]]; [[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16-17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16-17]]; [[Ecclesiastes 12:13 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 12:13]]; [[1 Timothy 1:5 >> Bible:1 Timothy 1:5]]; [[1 Corinthians 8:1-3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 8:1-3]]; [[1 Corinthians 13:2 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:2]]; [[James 1:22-25 >> Bible:James 1:22-25]]; [[Revelation 22:14 >> Bible:Revelation 22:14]]).

Second, from the first intention and the internal end, which in reality are the same. That discipline whose first intention and last internal end is practical is a practical habit. But the first intention and last internal end of sacred theology is practical. Therefore sacred theology is a practical habit. The major is plain. The minor is proved first from the first reason, because from the testimonies recited it is clear that theology aims at faith, which is effective through love ([[Galatians 5:6 >> Bible:Galatians 5:6]]) and produces the fruit of good works that conform to the divine law in the worship of God and the love of neighbor.

Next, that theology also aims at and regards the generation and confirmation of faith, and the amendment of life as the fruit of faith, is proved from the last external end — namely eternal life — to which we can come only through faith as the apprehending means. That act by which alone a person is led to eternal life is first intended by theology. But faith is that act by which alone a person is led to eternal life, as will be proved below in its place. Therefore faith is first intended by theology.

title: Third and fourth proofs from practical means and the mode of the primary object; theology is a practical habit
english: 9. Third, from practical means. That discipline whose means do not stop in theory but extend themselves to practice is a practical habit. But the means of sacred theology do not stop in theory; they extend themselves to practice. Therefore sacred theology is a practical habit. The major shines with its own light. The minor is proved because the Word of God and the sacraments, by which the Holy Spirit works and confirms faith, do not stop in bare speculation but are handed down for the sake of something else ([[1 Timothy 1:5 >> Bible:1 Timothy 1:5]]; [[1 Timothy 4:1 >> Bible:1 Timothy 4:1]] and following).

10. Fourth, from the mode of the primary object. That discipline which does not know its primary object merely in order to know it, but in order to do something about what is known — that is, to worship God by loving him above all things, to correct and humble itself in order to him, and to love the neighbor in order to the same as itself, by building him up — is a practical habit. But sacred theology does not know its primary object merely in order to know it, but in order to do something about what is known. Therefore sacred theology is a practical habit.

11. From all these things it is indeed plain that sacred theology is a practical habit: for it is known not merely in order that it may be known, remaining shut within the intellect in cognition — which is the specific difference of theoretical disciplines, by which they are distinguished from practical ones — but also so that it may extend itself beyond the intellect, namely so that the will may rest in the object known by the intellect: that is, may by faith apprehend the grace of God offered, may love the offering God above all things and the rest in order to him and for his sake, and may set its hope in him — which is altogether a practical discipline.

And a heap of divine testimonies may be brought forward by which this discipline is praised not only as prudence but also as wisdom, as may be seen in ([[Proverbs 7:4 >> Bible:Proverbs 7:4]]; [[James 3:17 >> Bible:James 3:17]]) and many others, both elsewhere and in the Theological Precognita of Master Alsted and in the Syntagma of Doctor Polanus.

title: Four objections: theology holds theorems; the practical object is the doable; it treats theory as well as practice; eternal life is cognition
english: Next, someone may object that theology contains many theorems — God is; God is one; God is infinitely perfect — and very many like them handed down by us ourselves in theology, from which he gathers this: the object of a practical discipline is the doable (τὸ πρακτόν), which can be produced by us; the object of theology is not the doable which can be produced by us; therefore theology is not a practical discipline. The minor is proved because the object of theology is God and divine things.

Third, someone may take exception: theology does not treat only of practice, that is, of the worship of God, but also of theory or the knowledge of God. Therefore it is not only practical but also theoretical.

Fourth, someone may bring forward: the eternal life that theology sets forth is situated in the knowledge of God ([[John 17:3 >> Bible:John 17:3]]). Therefore theology is rather theoretical than practical. The reason of the consequence is that cognition is an act of the intellect and looks to theory.

title: Replies to the first and second objections: Hebrew wise for just; theorems ordered to practice; the doable in itself or in another
english: 13. We reply to the first. First, it is not yet clear whether those places treat of sacred theology as a discipline methodically shaped and arranged — which is the question here — and so a doubt is proved by an equally doubtful thing. Second, even if we liberally grant that these and other sayings of Scripture alleged for this matter treat of sacred theology as such, they still do not prove it non-practical but theoretical, or at least partly theoretical and partly practical — which is what those who differ from us separately desire. For those places more carefully inspected show a Hebraism by which wise is frequently used in Scripture for the prudent and the just, because he is described almost everywhere from just actions. So also the whole book of Proverbs uses the word wisdom everywhere. From chapter 10 verse 11 the most learned Thomas Cartwright says on this place that he who is here called wise appears to be called just, so that he who, justified by faith, does not cultivate righteousness is not truly to be counted wise.

Yet in truth, even if some documents in theology, considered in themselves and by themselves, are theorems of things proposed to be known: still, when related and weighed, as is fair, to their whole as parts of theology and to its last end, all are theorems of manners or practical monuments — for they are handed down not only to be known or contemplated, but to be referred to the worship of God and the salvation of man. Hence by a notable theoretical science of God and divine things hypocrites and the ungodly are made no better or happier. Truly Justin Martyr: our religion consists not in words but in deeds. If that respect is neglected and set aside, no practical discipline at all will be given, because there is no practice that does not include some knowledge.

14. In the first syllogism we distinguish the major. For the object of a practical discipline is the doable, either in itself and its nature, or in another which, though distinct from the object, is so joined to it that the object is known and the discipline treated for its sake. Minor is not true. For although God in himself and his nature    is not the doable, yet the simply first and necessary end, and the justification of his name, for which he is proposed to be known in theology, is the doable. John Duns Scotus (on the Sentences book 1 question 4) asserts that even these theological propositions — God is triune; the Father begets the Son; the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit — are practical, because they virtually include the knowledge of the rightness of love tending to the three persons of the Deity, none excluded. As for divine things, some are from God alone, as the works of creation and redemption; others principally from God and secondarily, in a certain respect, also from man, insofar as human actions also concur toward them — as faith, justification, sanctification, and the whole worship of God. The former are referred to the doable in the way God is; the latter are such in themselves and their nature.

title: Replies to the third and fourth objections; Gerhard on practical theology; orthodoxy and Christian life
english: 15. To the third, we deny the consequence, because not just any cognition makes a theoretical discipline, but only that which does not of itself direct to practice. But the theological knowledge of God of itself directs a person to the practice of piety.

16. To the fourth, we deny the consequence. Eternal life consists in cognition not as in an end, but as in a means to the end, without which no adult attains the end — namely his salvation and the sanctification of God's name. Doctor Johannes Gerhard, professor at Jena, agrees with us among others in the preface to his Meditations. It is agreed, he says, that theology is a practical doctrine, and therefore those think less rightly who contend that it is speculative, among whom are some of the scholastics. For although not only things to be done, but also things to be believed and hoped, are proposed in this heavenly philosophy, that still does not hinder its still being called practical. For medicine too is occupied with the theory of certain things, and yet is not therefore a theoretical discipline, because it pursues that very theory by reason of practice and in order to practice: the same applies to theology that in those very things to be believed, or in the articles of faith, not bare knowledge but also assent is required, which those to whom this care belongs confirm by arguments to be an act on the will's side. But if theology is a practical doctrine, then surely its end also will not be bare knowledge and subtle theory, but rather practice. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them, says the Savior to the disciples. The strength of our religion consists not in words but in deeds, says Justin. The sum of religion is to imitate him whom you worship, says Augustine. If therefore the end and perfection of the Christian religion is not bare knowledge but practice, how few will you find today who are truly Christians! Everywhere much science, little conscience. It is most right that orthodoxy is defended by books, disputations, sermons, and every means: but care must also be taken that life answer to the Christian profession. Thus Doctor Gerhard.

title: Sacred theology is not among Aristotle's five logical virtues; spiritual things differ in kind from natural disciplines
english: 17. Sacred theology, truly and properly speaking, cannot be referred to any of the five logical virtues that Aristotle explains in Nicomachean Ethics book 6, because the things it considers differ in kind — or by their whole nature and condition — from those things from whose variety and unequal nature those five habits of mind and their ends and aims are deduced.

For the three theoretical perfections or habits turn about necessary things, whose knowledge can be searched out by the keenness of the human mind without the Word of God: the knowledge of spiritual things cannot without the Word of God. Contingent things, of which some fall under our action and others under our making, are placed in our power and were first searched out by human study and industry, so that they can be acquired. Hence civil happiness in Ethics book 1 is everywhere called a human good.

But spiritual things are by no means in a person's power and cannot be acquired at his choice: they either are in us by generation from corrupt seed, as original sin, which is the peculiar disease of the animal human being brought forth into light by natural procreation from the corrupt; or they are God-given (θεόδοτον), that is, they come from heaven by mere grace and mercy — as true conversion to God, faith, remission of sins, regeneration, and so on.

Although this discipline, which must be held most firmly, considers spiritual things, and is therefore diverse in whole kind from the other disciplines called theoretical, practical, or productive: still with those called practical and productive it has no small analogy.

title: Analogy with practical arts: fixed end, subject, and exact definition of the end as justification
english: 1. For just as in practical — and even in productive — disciplines a certain end is set forth, which is the measure and norm of all the other things considered in them, by which it can be known what belongs to them by right of property and what is more or less ancillary and foreign to them: so also theology has a certain end, about which none of those who in every age have been engaged in this kind of study has ever doubted — namely righteousness before God, which whether you call it before God, or remission of sins, or the inheritance of eternal life, or salvation, or by whatever other name, so long as you understand the thing itself, nothing more concerns this our design.

2. Just as in practical disciplines it is usual to consider the subject set under the end that comes — namely the human being — so the human being under vice is no less necessary in this discipline than the human body and its parts in medicine, and without doubt a hundred thousand times more necessary because of the greatness of the most atrocious spiritual disease of all human beings, plainly hidden beneath reason.

3. Just as in practical disciplines and arts it is supremely necessary that the definition of the end itself, which is the principle of cognition, be constituted most accurately — whence Aristotle carefully warns both about this and about other principles near the end of Nicomachean Ethics book 1 chapter 7 that care must be taken that they be rightly defined, since they have great force for what follows — so in sacred theology the most exact definition of the end, or of justification and eternal life, must be sought from the sacred letters.

Hence almost a thousand times Doctor Luther and other orthodox theologians inculcate in their writings, nearly to nausea, that if the article of justification is lost, the whole Christian doctrine is lost at once; likewise that whoever deny the article of justification at once take CHRIST out of the midst; likewise that when the article of justification is known we walk in clearest light, and when it is unknown in densest darkness; likewise that when this one article is well constituted and known the papacy is overthrown. The reason of these assertions is twofold. First, because the justification of the sinful human being before God is the end for whose sake the whole of sacred Scripture has been disclosed from heaven, and so the aim of our whole theology, which for this end is learned in the schools, taught in the church, and practiced. Second, because if this end is not well constituted and defined, those things cannot be rightly known which have been ordained from heaven for attaining the end and prescribed to us in theology as the speech of the kingdom.

title: From the defined end come the means, chiefly faith; theology differs from other disciplines in end, means, and subject
english: Just as in practical disciplines from the notion or well-constituted definition of the end the means leading to the end are elicited and known — and especially those nearer the attaining of the end, as Aristotle teaches (Posterior Analytics book 1 chapter 2; Ethics book 1 toward the beginning of the last chapter) — so also in theology, when justification is well known and accurately defined, that nearest means is more easily known by which alone sinners are made righteous before God, namely faith, which rests on God's mercy and the merit of our Savior Jesus Christ.

I say the nearest means, because there are also others a little more remote, such as the preaching and hearing of the heavenly Word and the use of the sacraments, by which God gathers a Church for himself, the Holy Spirit is effectual, and by the sermon of the law, as by lightning and thunder, strikes consciences and leads them into the acknowledgment of their sins, while he stirs true grief for having offended God. But by the voice of the Gospel he again soothes those struck and as it were raises them from spiritual death and kindles and confirms true faith; by which alone, apprehending God's mercy and Christ's merit, sinners are made righteous before God and are brought into his obedience.

Yet lest anyone be deceived by these analogies and likenesses, our most august sacred theology — of which we dare to pronounce with better right and more truly than Aristotle of his, from Metaphysics book 3 chapter 2, that it is most princely and mistress, to which it is unlawful for the others, as handmaids, to contradict — differs from the others in this: (1) that the end of the others, and the means leading to the end, are of our choice; but by no means are the end and means of sacred theology of the choice of our old Adam; (2) that the subject of the other disciplines also contributes something to the end; but the subject of this one, the sinful human being, contributes plainly nothing. For the Holy Spirit wholly effects the conversion of the sinful human being and kindles the faith by which alone he is made righteous before God.

Although theological learning, insofar as it is common to the holy and the unholy, admits a certain comparison with philosophical habits: yet prophecy, since it is called the gift of understanding and explaining Scripture ([[1 Corinthians 14:1 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:1]] and following), rests on its own singular and proper principles and rules.

title: IV. Whether sacred theology is the same as the habit of faith and piety; science and wisdom
english: IV. Is sacred theology therefore the same as the habit of faith and piety? Faith is a practical habit, and can rightly be called a doctrine or discipline objectively, according to that word of Christ ([[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]): Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me. For the object of faith is taught by God and learned by human beings: and without this no one is pleasing to God or is saved ([[Hebrews 11:6 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:6]]; [[Mark 16:16 >> Bible:Mark 16:16]]).

But sacred theology is another habit, which deduces, explains, confirms the articles of faith from their principles and foundations, and defends them against adversaries. Although this habit is not in all the faithful, yet it is uniquely required by the Apostle in a teacher of the Church ([[1 Corinthians 12:1 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:1]] and following). Without this habit many please God and are saved, as unlearned believers: and with this habit, if it is without faith and the struggle of the Spirit, many displease God and are condemned, as unbelieving teachers, hypocrites, seditious wranglers, and tyrants ([[Matthew 7:21 >> Bible:Matthew 7:21]]–23; [[Matthew 23:2 >> Bible:Matthew 23:2]], 13, 15; [[Luke 11:52 >> Bible:Luke 11:52]]). Compare the illustration of blessed Augustine (On the Trinity book 14 chapter 1) explaining ([[1 Corinthians 12:8 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:8]]).

The schools wrongly distinguish science from faith, yet with a praiseworthy intention. For faith is knowledge ([[Isaiah 53:11 >> Bible:Isaiah 53:11]]). And one must glory in this knowledge as in a gift diverse from worldly knowledge ([[Jeremiah 9:23 >> Bible:Jeremiah 9:23]]). The scholastics meant to teach that Christian faith is not produced by demonstrations that produce human science, because faith is of things not seen and does not rest on philosophical principles or things known by nature. And this is not badly but usefully warned, insofar as theological faith is discerned from philosophical science. Yet this also ought to have been observed: that sacred Scripture takes up philosophical science, as collapsing under its own mass in divine things, and rebuilds what has been made vain, new foundations laid under and new stays added, so that, cultivated from a sacred beginning, it may issue in faith vigorous with the strength of the Word because of God its author.

Experience teaches that whatever philosophers seem somehow to weave about God and divine things, the more curiously and accurately they try to establish it, the less at last they reach its end. And the Apostle rightly wrote ([[Romans 1:21 >> Bible:Romans 1:21]]): They became vain in their reasonings. Therefore the wisdom of the wise is abolished, and the understanding of the understanding is taken out of the midst.

Further, from ([[1 John 2:3 >> Bible:1 John 2:3]]–4; [[1 John 3:6 >> Bible:1 John 3:6]]; [[1 Corinthians 8:1 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 8:1]]–2) it is easily understood that so great a science of sacred things consists in two things: (1) in the truth of a certain common and universal knowledge about the Word of God and the dogmas of the church; (2) and indeed chiefly in the efficacy of knowledge or in the truth of application, by which our mind rightly accommodates common principles and dogmas to things to be done and to singulars and discerns the things that are excellent ([[Philippians 1:10 >> Bible:Philippians 1:10]]; [[Philemon 1:6 >> Bible:Philemon 1:6]]; [[Ephesians 5:10 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:10]]) — that is, so that it may form a practical judgment about the things that occur to be done, which is truly consentaneous to the principles. Otherwise it happens that what we confess with the mouth we deny by deeds ([[Titus 1:16 >> Bible:Titus 1:16]]). That common knowledge, when destitute of efficacy, the Apostle calls puffing-up science: in respect of which whoever would think himself to know God is a liar if we believe John — having indeed a form of truth but denying its power ([[2 Timothy 3:5 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:5]]).

For this reason he is not sufficiently properly called a theologian, just as he is not properly called prudent in human affairs who, when he has understood common principles, rich in theory, either in no way or badly accommodates the same to singular counsels — as the most exact theologian Doctor Conrad Bergius, my most sincere colleague, truly discusses in the Precognita on Loci Communes Theology, chapter on the internal form of theology, and thence wisely gathers two things: (1) that theology can indeed be true even which an ungodly person possesses, as to the truth of common knowledge; but as to application it will not be true but hypocritical; and Scripture in comparison with the science of the saints judges it unworthy of the name of science and therefore also of theology; (2) that one is a better theologian as to the breadth of science, another as to the efficacy of science — who without doubt is more approved by God.

We say that theology is science and wisdom, not speaking philosophically, but in a mode singularly fitted to this doctrine. For it differs from philosophical science and wisdom by principles not known of themselves; it is confirmed by the authority of God the teacher, to whom they are known of themselves; and it is inspired by a peculiar grace and power, yet through the Word. And that there is a difference of theological wisdom and science is plain from ([[1 Corinthians 12:8 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:8]]): through the Spirit to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge. This seems chiefly to be it: that science is taken of the cognition of doctrine, but wisdom of the skilled use of science ([[Job 28:28 >> Bible:Job 28:28]]; [[Proverbs 14:8 >> Bible:Proverbs 14:8]]; [[Proverbs 27:12 >> Bible:Proverbs 27:12]]).

title: V–VI. Philosophical names of habits are alien if taken strictly; theology's principles are from revelation, method from industry
english: V. Is the appellation of intelligence, science, wisdom, art, or prudence alien from the nature and definition of sacred theology? Altogether, if one prefers to speak of these habits agreeably to their philosophical definitions with Aristotle, the prince of philosophers — except for one spiritual prudence or faith, by which properly there is cognition of things pertaining to the kingdom of God, which is truly a practical habit and the genus of theology — also by the suffrage of him who writes publicly that theology is practical, not speculative, not by that common reason by which all arts and disciplines have their activity for an end, but especially concerning practice. But whoever attributes all these appellations to one sacred theology not popularly but properly in an accurate and philosophical kind of speech, by the same work attributes contradictory differences to the same defined thing, which we taught to be absurd in question 2 number 4. Nor does the contrary reason bind — namely that all these things are in any accurate discipline. For both the nature of disciplines distinguished from one another by opposite differences, and the whole chorus of the best philosophers, refute this. Otherwise, when the object of theology is taken in such breadth that it embraces whatever things are in the nature of things created and ordered by God, insofar as they are to be referred to God as to their principle and end, even Physics, Ethics, Politics, and other disciplines are contained within the terms of theology — as the most celebrated theologian of the Leiden Academy, Doctor Johannes Polyander, observes from Augustine's letter to Volusianus (Synopsis of purer theology, disputation 1 thesis 12).

VI. Whether sacred theology is from nature and human habit of inquiry, as the remaining disciplines, or rather from divine revelation and institution? A distinction must be made between the principles, the things underlying sacred theology, and the methodical explanation, demonstration, and disposition of principles, things, and conclusions deduced from them.

As to the former: the principles of other disciplines, innate to us, can be expressed and brought to perfection by sense, observation, induction, and experience, as among others Verulam shows eruditely in many places in the Great Instauration. But the solid and native principles of sacred theology, which by human study and industry can be advanced to perfection, are not in us by nature, nor are they found by the powers of nature ([[Matthew 16:17 >> Bible:Matthew 16:17]]); but they are learned from divine revelation and institution ([[Isaiah 54:13 >> Bible:Isaiah 54:13]]; [[Matthew 11:27 >> Bible:Matthew 11:27]]; [[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]; [[Galatians 1:11 >> Bible:Galatians 1:11]]–12). Compare chapter 2 aph. 5.

As to the latter: it hangs upon human industry and reasoning applied more or less according to the measure of grace, after the manner of the other disciplines, as is abundantly plain enough from the most published methods of sacred theology, of which some are more, others less, exact.

title: VII. The proper subject of sacred theology is the kingdom of God, and man as subject to God unto beatitude
english: VII. What is the proper subject of sacred theology? Answer. 1. In the schools Thomas (part 1 question 1 article 7) makes God the subject, not taking the word practically, as Lord, prince, and king of the universe, but theoretically, so that the first being is signified: but he rests on the false hypothesis that theology is rather theoretical than practical. Nearer the truth among Gregory of Valencia (disputation 1 question 1 point 3 paragraph 5) are Hugh of St. Victor, who makes the works of reparation the subject; Durandus, who makes God as Savior; Bonaventure, who makes the mystical body of Christ with its head — that is, Christ himself and the Church; and the Riminese, who makes God as glorifier or as rewarder. But they restrict the subject too much. For Bonaventure assigns only the object of evangelical doctrine: the rest act as if someone constituted the prince rather than the commonwealth the subject of politics.

2. But from the sayings ([[Mark 1:14 >> Bible:Mark 1:14]]–15; [[Matthew 4:23 >> Bible:Matthew 4:23]]; [[Luke 9:2 >> Bible:Luke 9:2]]; [[Acts 28:23 >> Bible:Acts 28:23]], 31; [[Matthew 13:11 >> Bible:Matthew 13:11]]) it is gathered that most simply and most fittingly to the Scriptures the subject of theological doctrine — what they call the subject of treatment — is said to be the kingdom of God in general, as the kingdom of grace in species is the subject of the Gospel, which Jesus Christ, the fountain of all theology, taught and commanded his Apostles to teach.

3. So the material object is all things that can in any way be reduced to the kingdom of God. 4. But the subject is considered otherwise in practical than in theoretical disciplines: in these its principles and affections are sought for the sake of science; in those, insofar as it is laid under some operation. 5. The formal reason of the object, which is primarily considered in theology, is the same with the form of the kingdom, and they are the very moral acts by which the kingdom of God consists — of which sort are, on God's side, creation, redemption, and sanctification; from which also arise faith, hope, and charity on the human side, and what can be reduced to those, as helping or instrumental causes, as the Church, the magistrate, the sacraments. Whence also the formal reason is sought from the determination of the theological habit or knowledge, so that the object is the kingdom of God: (1) insofar as it is revealed from heaven, which determination is from the principle or efficient cause of knowledge; (2) insofar as it is revealed unto human salvation, which determination is from the end of revelation and knowledge. From which it is concluded that not all things are taught in theology that pertain in any way to the kingdom of God, but those useful to human beings for piety and eternal life ([[Titus 3:1 >> Bible:Titus 3:1]] and following; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]–17; [[Isaiah 48:17 >> Bible:Isaiah 48:17]]).

6. But since sacred theology has been granted to us that it may lead a human being under God's rule to the simply highest good and most absolute beatitude, it is clear that its subject also is the human being insofar as he can be subjected to God, made God-minded (θεοῦνουν), conformed to the divine will, and come to eternal life. 7–9. As in theoretical disciplines restriction of the subject is sought from the mode of considering, so in practical ones from the end; and not whatever can be known about the subject need be handed down, but only what makes for attaining the end. 10. Therefore since here the subject is the human being as to be subjected to God his king, conformed to the divine will, and saved, it contributes nothing to the end if he is considered as a natural body endowed with natural principles and affections: but here it is taught how, blessed at the beginning by God Most High unto eternal life, he was deprived of it by the fraud and malice of Satan, what he wholly was after the fall, and into what miseries he was cast headlong, so that we may more easily and clearly know by what means he is freed and saved by God's grace from the dominion of sin and eternal ruin.

11. Therefore, to conclude at last, the proper subject of theology is the human being insofar as he is subjected to God his king, conformed, and beatified by him: but the primary yet partial subject is the human heart or intellect and will, in which God reigns, because the life of God is the spiritual act of the whole human being by which he is borne to God rightly known as his king to be held and to be acted according to his will. That this act is proper to the will freed by the grace of Christ from the slavery of sin is agreed ([[Proverbs 4:23 >> Bible:Proverbs 4:23]]; [[Proverbs 23:26 >> Bible:Proverbs 23:26]]; [[Psalm 110:3 >> Bible:Psalm 110:3]]).

title: VIII–IX. Theology does not swallow ethics and politics; metaphysics and ethics do not vanish but serve
english: VIII. Because there is truly nothing in theology that is not referred to the last end, or to means looking to that end, of which kind all things tend directly to practice — does it follow that that practice of life is so perfectly contained in theology that there is no precept of catholic truth in economics, ethics, politics, or jurisprudence looking to living well that does not properly look to theology? Although someone affirms this, we nevertheless do not dare to assent to him in this, because he dangerously confounds and restricts useful — indeed necessary — and in whole kind different disciplines of the light of nature and of grace, as a cook confuses a great cauldron, when it only boils, with a small ladle. Economics, ethics, politics, and jurisprudence are indeed disciplines:   even if they contain precepts of catholic truth — or, what is the same, things universally, of themselves, and reciprocally true, and pertaining to living well — yet they were both invented and cultivated under the light of nature, and under the page of this light they attain their proper end: and although they also borrow many things from the sacred letters and under the light of grace and of Christianity attain a greater eminence and are ordered and corrected unto theological perfection: still they are distinguished in whole kind from sacred theology, which under the revealed light of grace promises eternal life above the force and light of nature. The Gospel of Christ does not take away polities, says the pious soul Philip Melanchthon. We in like manner: Theology does not take away philosophy and jurisprudence, but lifts both up and directs them to the service of Christ.

IX. Do metaphysics and ethics, after they have given testimony to the distribution of theology into faith and observance, vanish of their own accord? 1. There is a learned man who publicly teaches that from the remains of those two parts two theologies have sprung up among certain philosophers, metaphysics and ethics, because metaphysics is the faith of the Peripatetics and ethics their observance. Hence, he says, they attribute to each of these disciplines that they hand down the highest human good. About ethics this is known to all; about metaphysics, which they also call theology, Francis Suárez (disputation 1 section 5 number 43): In the most perfect situation of metaphysics, he says, human beatitude consists. It contemplates the highest good and the last end simply. Divine contemplation formally or elicitively pertains to this science.

2. But in truth neither metaphysics vanishes nor ethics, even if both give testimony to sacred theology. For no one of sound mind has accepted that the light of nature is destroyed and extinguished by the light of grace. The natural faculty of reasoning is not killed by supernatural and divine faith but is perfected, ordered to spiritual things, and sublimated. 3. Nor have philosophers properly made two theologies from these disciplines, although they have sometimes called metaphysics theology, because it also treats of the first being, which by the most common concept of all is God. For the rest it supplies principles to dialectical disputations, as the remaining sciences do to analytics and demonstrations: and therefore metaphysics is no more to be called faith than other sciences. 4. The highest moral good that ethics intends with the remaining practical disciplines, and the natural that metaphysics intends with the remaining theoretical disciplines, differs from the spiritual that sacred theology intends, as that which is in a qualified way and in its own kind — that is, in the sphere of nature, in which God as first being and simply highest is known under the light of nature somehow congruently with nature's powers — from that which is absolutely highest, namely God revealed through Holy Scripture or the Gospel, to be most perfectly known and worshiped in the kingdom of grace and glory. 5. From which we gather that sacred theology does not take these noblest parts of philosophy out of the midst, but rejoices in their obedience and service, and feeds, emends, fosters, and sanctifies them into these.

title: X. The end of sacred theology: internal and external; the life of God; four grades of life; Cap. 1 close
english: X. What is the END of sacred theology? 1. The end of sacred theology is considered as twofold, internal and external. The internal is to teach the sacred mysteries and dogmas from the Scriptures — that is, to explain, demonstrate, and defend them rightly — unto exciting the life of God in the hearers. The external is the life of God, by which we are united, subjected, and obedient to our creator, redeemer, and sanctifier in light ([[Ephesians 4:17 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:17]]–18), or human beatitude begun, which is of faith, then consummated, which is of vision or eternal life, by which it is well with us in the way and in the fatherland in God, and by him we are nourished, strengthened, and refreshed as by our last real personal end ([[Genesis 15:1 >> Bible:Genesis 15:1]]).

2. This life, one and the same as to essence, remains from its beginning unto eternity ([[John 3:36 >> Bible:John 3:36]]; [[John 5:24 >> Bible:John 5:24]]; [[1 John 3:15 >> Bible:1 John 3:15]]). 3. And to live to God and to Christ ([[Romans 6:10 >> Bible:Romans 6:10]]–11) and to righteousness ([[1 Peter 2:24 >> Bible:1 Peter 2:24]]) is to direct all our actions and operations of faith and of life according to God's will unto God's glory, and to serve him in them, God himself acting within. 4. So we are said to live according to the flesh ([[Romans 8:12 >> Bible:Romans 8:12]]–13) — that is, to institute and carry out all our actions at the pleasure of original malice. Contrary to this is to live by the Spirit ([[Galatians 5:25 >> Bible:Galatians 5:25]]), to live justly, soberly, piously ([[Titus 2:12 >> Bible:Titus 2:12]]), no longer to live the remaining time in the flesh to human lusts but to the will of God, and to live according to God, that is, by the Spirit ([[1 Peter 4:2 >> Bible:1 Peter 4:2]], 6). So Paul ([[Galatians 2:19 >> Bible:Galatians 2:19]]–20): that I may live to God, he says, I have been crucified together with Christ — that is, I have been mortified, or my old Adam has been slain and a new one founded in me, that thereafter I may serve God by the Spirit of newness ([[2 Corinthians 4:10 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 4:10]]; [[Philippians 1:20 >> Bible:Philippians 1:20]]).

5. The life of GOD — not that by which God himself lives, who is life itself, but that by which we are made alive by him, or rather live — can be taken twofold ([[Ephesians 4:18 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:18]]): either that which is counted before God, as the glory of God ([[John 12:43 >> Bible:John 12:43]]), the righteousness of God ([[Romans 10:3 >> Bible:Romans 10:3]]–4, 6) by the grace of evangelical justification; or that which God communicates to us by the spirit of regeneration. 6. Whichever way you take it, the sense is the same. For this common life by which we are human beings, compared to the life of God, is nothing other than an empty image of life, not only because it quickly passes, but also because our souls are dead while living when they do not cling to God.

7. And there occur in this world four grades of life. For one is most common, which consists only in vigor, which belongs also to plants and the vegetable kingdom and by the Paracelsists is stretched also to the mineral kingdom. Another is universal, which consists in motion and sense, of which beasts also are partakers — which Thomas Campanella in his books on the sense of things extends to all parts of the world and the particles of parts. The third is human, by which we are sons of Adam. But the fourth is supernatural, which the faithful alone obtain. 8. All these grades of life are from God, and therefore can loosely be called the life of God. Of the first and second grade there is ([[Acts 17:28 >> Bible:Acts 17:28]]). But the fourth by excellence — the regeneration of the faithful, which is the principle of eternal life — is here named the life of God, because then God properly lives in us, and we enjoy his life, when he governs us by his Spirit, according to that ([[Romans 8:10 >> Bible:Romans 8:10]]–14): If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also make alive your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, it will be that you die: but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are sons of God.
